etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English patroun, patrone, from Old French patron, from Latin patrōnus, derived from pater (“father”). Doublet of padrone, Patronus, patroon, and pattern.

definitions.definition: A guardian or intercessor; synonym of patron saint.
One who protects or supports; a defender or advocate.

quote.citation: c. 1590–1592 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Taming of the Shrew”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act IV, scene ii]:
quote.text: patron of my life and liberty

quote.citation: 1590, Edmund Spenser, “Book I, Canto I”, in The Faerie Queene. […], London:  […]  [John Wolfe] for William Ponsonbie, →OCLC:
1834–1838 (date written), Thomas Babington Macaulay, “Virginia”, in Lays of Ancient Rome, London: Longman, Brown, Green, and Longmans, […], published 1842, →OCLC, page 154:
quote.text: Let him who works the client wrong beware the patron’s ire!

definitions.definition: An influential, wealthy person who supported an artist, craftsman, a scholar or a noble.
A customer, as of a certain store or restaurant.

quote.citation: 2019, Li Huang, James Lambert, “Another Arrow for the Quiver: A New Methodology for Multilingual Researchers”, in Journal of Multilingual and Multicultural Development, →DOI, page 4:
quote.text: In our trial of the AOT, a transect was used to collect data about the languages being spoken by patrons of the NIE cafeteria during lunchtimes.

definitions.definition: (historical, Roman law) A protector of a dependent, especially a master who had freed a slave but still retained some paternal rights.
(UK, ecclesiastical) One who has gift and disposition of a benefice.
(obsolete or historical) A property owner, a landlord, a master. (Compare patroon.)

quote.citation: 1879, Annie Allnutt Brassey, A Voyage in the "Sunbeam", page 170:
quote.text: Half-a-dozen little boys carried it to the inn, where I had to explain to the patron, in my best Spanish, that we wanted a carriage to go to the baths, seven leagues off.

quote.citation: 1992, Eric O. Ayisi, St. Eustatius, Treasure Island of the Caribbean:
quote.text: [...] would obtain permission from the West India Company to settle in certain areas in the New World and cultivate the land. Sometimes absentee patrons would give the colony to a group of interested persons and the patrons would finance ...

definitions.definition: (transitive, obsolete) To be a patron of; to patronize; to favour.

quote.citation: 1642, Tho[mas] Browne, “(please specify the page)”, in Religio Medici. […], 4th edition, London:  […]  E. Cotes for Andrew Crook […], published 1656, →OCLC:
quote.text: a good cause needs not to be patroned by passion

definitions.definition: (transitive, obsolete) To treat as a patron.
